the results of this series of experiments are not in line with a theory of inductive reasoning based on the notion of a “mental model” or “cognitive routine.”
Simpson’s paradox is a difficult task for lay people, but not impossible.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inductive reasoning in a situation like Simpson’s paradox can be improved when participants are made more aware of the covariate and when the causal role of the covariate is made more salient.
the cognitive processes involved in the assessment of trivariate relationships are complex and can be easily disrupted by judgment interference.

inductive reasoning in the social domain is prone to interference from the gender stereotype, and that the interference effect can be reduced when the salience and causal status of covariates is increased and the salience of social categories is decreased.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the paradoxical nature of Simpson’s paradox can be a source of cognitive bias in judgment and decision making, but that it is possible to mitigate such biases through the use of appropriate contextual cues.
inductive inference is often biased by the availability of information and by the salience of covariates.
inductive reasoning is not a unitary process.
